name: Consumer Surplus Loss from a Tariff or Quota
expression: CS loss = ΔP × Qd_r + ½ × ΔP × (Qd_ft − Qd_r)
meaning: The magnitude of consumer surplus lost when a tariff or equivalent quota raises the domestic price from the world price to the restricted price.

variables.ΔP: the domestic price increase caused by the restriction (Pt − P*)
variables.Qd_r: domestic quantity demanded after the restriction (at the higher price Pt)
variables.Qd_ft: domestic quantity demanded under free trade (at the world price P*)

intuition: This is the trapezoid area under the demand curve between the free-trade and restricted price levels: a rectangle for the units still consumed after the restriction, plus a triangle for the consumption that is priced out entirely.
commonMistake: Using the free-trade quantity instead of the restricted quantity in the rectangle term, which overstates the loss.
relatedLearningOutcome: compare types of trade restrictions, such as tariffs, quotas, and export subsidies, and their economic implications

name: Producer Surplus Gain from a Tariff or Quota
expression: PS gain = ΔP × Qs_ft + ½ × ΔP × (Qs_r − Qs_ft)
meaning: The magnitude of producer surplus gained by domestic producers when a tariff or equivalent quota raises the domestic price.

variables.ΔP: the domestic price increase caused by the restriction (Pt − P*)
variables.Qs_ft: domestic quantity supplied under free trade (at the world price P*)
variables.Qs_r: domestic quantity supplied after the restriction (at the higher price Pt)

intuition: This is the area under the higher restricted price and above the supply curve: a rectangle on the output producers were already making, plus a triangle on the additional, higher-cost output the higher price draws into production.
commonMistake: Applying the restricted quantity instead of the free-trade quantity in the rectangle term, which overstates the gain.
relatedLearningOutcome: compare types of trade restrictions, such as tariffs, quotas, and export subsidies, and their economic implications

name: Tariff Revenue or Quota Rent
meaning: The value of the restriction's price wedge applied to the units still imported after the restriction: government tariff revenue for a tariff, or quota rent for a quota.

variables.ΔP: the domestic price increase caused by the restriction (Pt − P*)
variables.Qd_r: domestic quantity demanded after the restriction
variables.Qs_r: domestic quantity supplied after the restriction

intuition: Qd_r − Qs_r is the quantity still imported after the restriction; multiplying by the price wedge gives the value transferred on those units — captured by the government under a tariff, and ambiguously by the government, domestic importers, or foreign exporters under a quota.
commonMistake: Treating this amount as a net loss to the country rather than a transfer, when the recipient is domestic (government, under a tariff, or domestic license-holders, under an auctioned quota).
relatedLearningOutcome: compare types of trade restrictions, such as tariffs, quotas, and export subsidies, and their economic implications

name: Deadweight Loss from a Tariff or Quota
expression: Deadweight loss = ½ × ΔP × (Qs_r − Qs_ft) + ½ × ΔP × (Qd_ft − Qd_r)
meaning: The irreducible national welfare loss from a tariff or quota — the portion of the consumer surplus loss that is not offset by any domestic producer or government gain.

variables.ΔP: the domestic price increase caused by the restriction (Pt − P*)
variables.Qs_ft: domestic quantity supplied under free trade
variables.Qs_r: domestic quantity supplied after the restriction
variables.Qd_ft: domestic quantity demanded under free trade
variables.Qd_r: domestic quantity demanded after the restriction

intuition: The first triangle is production-side inefficiency (resources drawn into production that costs more than the world price); the second triangle is consumption-side inefficiency (mutually beneficial purchases that no longer occur). Together they are the country's national welfare loss regardless of who captures the revenue-or-rent term.
commonMistake: Omitting one of the two triangles (production-side or consumption-side) and reporting only half the true deadweight loss.
relatedLearningOutcome: compare types of trade restrictions, such as tariffs, quotas, and export subsidies, and their economic implications
